Its average push there is `(-0.38, -0.04)`: sideways, with almost no upward component. With the true labels it is `(-0.14, +0.99)`, straight up into B. So inside A∩B, guidance toward B has stopped meaning "more B". Contention: where a chimera comes from214# ### 4b. Contention: where a chimera comes from215#216# Read the two coordinates as **two slots in an image**. A cat is the value $-0.5$ in some slot, and a dog is $+0.5$ in some slot. The other slot holds anything.217#218# - **Centred training data**: every cat image has its cat in slot 1, and so does every dog image. Both experts constrain the same slot, so the product is a product over the same variables where a partition was meant. Its mass sits at $x_1 \approx 0$, a value that is neither cat nor dog. **That is the chimera.** For Gaussians the arithmetic is exact: $\mathcal{N}(-0.5, s^2)\,\mathcal{N}(+0.5, s^2) \propto \mathcal{N}(0, s^2/2)$.219# - **Position-varied training data**: each object appears in either slot. Interaction: wet dog245# **Reading it.** The operator is the same in both rows. What changed is **whether each expert's training data showed its object in more than one place.** So contention comes from the data: experts that never saw their object off-centre both claim the centre. In images, this predicts that cat-dog chimeras get rarer as the training data varies object position. That prediction is checkable.246#247# ### 4c. Interaction: wet dog248#249# B is rain: the top half, with any $x_1$. A is a dog. Inside the A∩B quadrant, A looks different: its $x_1$ shifts from $-0.5$ to $-0.8$ when B is present (the dog is wet). Everywhere else A sits at $x_1 \approx -0.5$.250#251# Separately trained experts see the shifted version only through the overlap in their training sets. The product puts its top-half mass near $x_1 = -0.5$, hugging the boundary $x_2 \approx 0$ where the dog expert's smoothed tail meets the rain: a dry dog at the edge of the rain. At 20% overlap, both experts hold some shifted points, and the product lands near $-0.8$. **The product found the interaction without any extra term, once the data contained it.** This is the evidence behind `break 7`: interaction may be intersection plus a data condition, rather than a third operator.277#278# ## What this notebook cannot show279#280# - **Nothing here was sampled.** Every product is exact on the grid. A real sampler (reverse diffusion or annealed MCMC) adds its own error, and that is claim 4.281# - **The experts are ideal.** A trained network extrapolates differently from Gaussian smoothing, and on images that extrapolation is the whole hope of claim 2. These figures show what the data permits, and say nothing about what a network invents.282# - **Two dimensions only.** "Slots" and "regions" are single coordinates here. Pixels in an image are not independent coordinates, and an object's region is not fixed.

Version 2 labels are used throughout.108 109# %% cell 6 [code]: B_set = np.array([[0.5, 0.5], [0.6, 0.4], [-0.4, 0.6]])110B_set = np.array([[0.5, 0.5], [0.6, 0.4], [-0.4, 0.6]])111pool = np.vstack([A_set, B_set])112label_sets = [{"A"}, {"A"}, {"A", "B"}, {"B"}, {"B"}, {"A", "B"}]113 114def condition(c, scheme):115    keep = [c in s if scheme == "contains" else s == {c} for s in label_sets]116    return pool[np.array(keep)]117 118sig = 0.15119lp_all = ideal_expert(pool, sig)120fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(10, 6.6))121for row, scheme in enumerate(["contains", "exactly"]):122    dA, dB = condition("A", scheme), condition("B", scheme)123    pA_c = density(ideal_expert(dA, sig)); pB_c = density(ideal_expert(dB, sig))124    comp = density(ideal_expert(dA, sig) + ideal_expert(dB, sig) - lp_all)125    show(ax[row, 0], pA_c, f'p(x|A), "{scheme}" A: {len(dA)} points\ntop-left mass {mass(pA_c, TOP_LEFT):.2f}', dA)126    show(ax[row, 1], pB_c, f'p(x|B), "{scheme}" B: {len(dB)} points\ntop-left mass {mass(pB_c, TOP_LEFT):.2f}', dB)127    show(ax[row, 2], comp, f'composed p(x|A)p(x|B)/p(x)\ntop-left mass {mass(comp, TOP_LEFT):.2f}')128plt.tight_layout()129 130# %% cell 7 [markdown]: 3. Break, part 2: a classifier learns the hidden-B points as "not B"134#135# Now a classifier $p(B\mid x)$ is trained, as in classifier guidance. Its labels come from **which set a point was in**, which is the label the data actually carries. A hidden-B point in A's set is therefore labelled "not B".136#137# Each set has 400 points. 20% of A's set lies in the top half (hidden B), and 20% of B's set lies in the left half (hidden A). The arrows show the direction of that push (unit length, so only direction is drawn), and the title gives its average over the top-left quadrant: $(+1, 0)$ is straight right, $(0, +1)$ straight up.138 139# %% cell 8 [code]: def make_sets(f, n=400):140def make_sets(f, n=400):141    a = np.c_[rng.uniform(-1, 0, n), np.where(rng.random(n) < f, rng.uniform(0, 1, n), rng.uniform(-1, 0, n))]142    b = np.c_[np.where(rng.random(n) < f, rng.uniform(-1, 0, n), rng.uniform(0, 1, n)), rng.uniform(0, 1, n)]143    return a, b144 145A400, B400 = make_sets(0.2)146X = np.vstack([A400, B400])147y_from_set = np.r_[np.zeros(400), np.ones(400)]          # the label the data carries148y_true = (X[:, 1] > 0).astype(float)                       # the label the concept defines149 150def train_classifier(X, y, steps=1500):151    torch.manual_seed(0)152    net = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(2, 64), torch.nn.SiLU(), torch.nn.Linear(64, 64), torch.nn.SiLU(), torch.nn.Linear(64, 1))153    opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), 3e-3, weight_decay=1e-3)154    Xt, yt = torch.tensor(X, dtype=torch.float32), torch.tensor(y, dtype=torch.float32)[:, None]155    for _ in range(steps):156        opt.zero_grad(); torch.nn.functional.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(net(Xt), yt).backward(); opt.step()157    return net158 159fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4.2))160q = np.linspace(-0.85, 0.85, 9); Q1, Q2 = np.meshgrid(q, q)161for a, y, name in [(ax[0], y_from_set, "labels from set membership"), (ax[1], y_true, "true labels (x2 > 0)")]:162    net = train_classifier(X, y)163    with torch.no_grad():164        pB = torch.sigmoid(net(torch.tensor(grid, dtype=torch.float32))).numpy().reshape(G, G)165    qx = torch.tensor(np.c_[Q1.ravel(), Q2.ravel()], dtype=torch.float32, requires_grad=True)166    torch.nn.functional.logsigmoid(net(qx)).sum().backward()167    gr = qx.grad.numpy(); gr = gr / (np.linalg.norm(gr, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-12)168    in_tl = (qx.detach().numpy()[:, 0] < 0) & (qx.detach().numpy()[:, 1] > 0)169    push = gr[in_tl].mean(0)170    a.imshow(pB, origin="lower", extent=[-L, L, -L, L], cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=1)171    a.quiver(Q1, Q2, gr[:, 0], gr[:, 1], color="w", scale=14, width=.006)172    a.axhline(0, c="w", lw=.4); Co-occurrence and intersection177# **Reading it.** With the labels the data carries, the classifier is unsure in the top-left quadrant, at about 0.5, because that quadrant holds equal numbers of hidden-B points labelled 0 and hidden-A points labelled 1. Its average push there is `(-0.38, -0.04)`: sideways, with almost no upward component. With the true labels it is `(-0.14, +0.99)`, straight up into B. So inside A∩B, guidance toward B has stopped meaning "more B". Its direction now follows where the label proportions happen to change (leftward toward the edge, rightward near $x_1 = 0$ into B-only), not the concept. **The classifier has learned part of "B" from where the points came from rather than from $x_2$, which is the toy's version of a shortcut**, like a pneumothorax classifier that reads the drain. With the true labels, the top-left quadrant is confidently B and the arrows point straight up.178#179# **Repaired claim 1.** A density expert learns its training set's density. The product keeps only where the two supports meet.192 193# %% cell 10 [code]: n = 2000194n = 2000195ring = lambda n: 0.5 * np.c_[np.cos(a := 2 * np.pi * rng.integers(0, 8, n) / 8), np.sin(a)] + 0.03 * rng.standard_normal((n, 2))196bar = lambda n: np.c_[rng.uniform(-0.2, 0.2, n), rng.uniform(-1, 1, n)]197left_half = lambda n: np.c_[rng.uniform(-1, 0, n), rng.uniform(-1, 1, n)]198top_half = lambda n: np.c_[rng.uniform(-1, 1, n), rng.uniform(0, 1, n)]199sub = lambda d: d[rng.choice(len(d), 600, replace=False)]   # subsample for speed on the grid200 201fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(10, 6.6))202for row, (fa, fb, na, nb_, region, rname) in enumerate([203        (left_half, top_half, "A: left half", "B: top half", TOP_LEFT, "top-left"),204        (ring, bar, "A: ring of 8", "B: vertical bar", (np.abs(X1) < 0.2) & (np.abs(np.hypot(X1, X2) - 0.5) < 0.1), "ring ∩ bar")]):205    lpA, lpB = ideal_expert(sub(fa(n)), 0.06), ideal_expert(sub(fb(n)), 0.06)206    show(ax[row, 0], density(lpA), na, region=None)207    show(ax[row, 1], density(lpB), nb_, region=None)208    prod = density(lpA + lpB)209    show(ax[row, 2], prod, f"product A·B\nmass in {rname} = {mass(prod, region):.2f}")210ax[0, 0].set_ylabel("co-occurrence"); ax[1, 0].set_ylabel("intersection")211plt.tight_layout()212 213# %% cell 11 [markdown]: 4b. Contention: where a chimera comes from214# ### 4b. Contention: where a chimera comes from215#216# Read the two coordinates as **two slots in an image**. A cat is the value $-0.5$ in some slot, and a dog is $+0.5$ in some slot. The other slot holds anything.217#218# - **Centred training data**: every cat image has its cat in slot 1, and so does every dog image. Both experts constrain the same slot, so the product is a product over the same variables where a partition was meant. Its mass sits at $x_1 \approx 0$, a value that is neither cat nor dog. **That is the chimera.** For Gaussians the arithmetic is exact: $\mathcal{N}(-0.5, s^2)\,\mathcal{N}(+0.5, s^2) \propto \mathcal{N}(0, s^2/2)$.219# - **Position-varied training data**: each object appears in either slot. The product now has modes at $(-0.5, +0.5)$ and $(+0.5, -0.5)$, one object per slot, both intact. **The same product operator produces co-occurrence.**220#221# The numbers: "co-occurrence" is the mass where one slot is within 0.15 of $-0.5$ and the other within 0.15 of $+0.5$. "Chimera" is the mass where neither slot is within 0.15 of either object.222 223# %% cell 12 [code]: def obj(v, n, varied):224def obj(v, n, varied):225    o = v + 0.05 * rng.standard_normal(n); other = rng.uniform(-1, 1, n)226    swap = (rng.random(n) < 0.5) if varied else np.zeros(n, bool)227    return np.where(swap[:, None], np.c_[other, o], np.c_[o, other])228 229near = lambda Z, v: np.abs(Z - v) < 0.15230CO = (near(X1, -.5) & near(X2, .5)) | (near(X1, .5) & near(X2, -.5))231CHIMERA = ~(near(X1, -.5) | near(X1, .5) | near(X2, -.5) | near(X2, .5))232 233fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(10, 6.6))234for row, varied in enumerate([False, True]):235    cat, dog = obj(-0.5, 600, varied), obj(0.5, 600, varied)236    lpc, lpd = ideal_expert(cat, 0.2), ideal_expert(dog, 0.2)237    show(ax[row, 0], density(lpc), f"cat expert ({'position-varied' if varied else 'centred'})", region=None)238    show(ax[row, 1], density(lpd), f"dog expert ({'position-varied' if varied else 'centred'})", region=None)239    prod = density(lpc + lpd)240    show(ax[row, 2], prod, f"product\nco-occurrence {mass(prod, CO):.2f} · chimera {mass(prod, CHIMERA):.2f}")241    for a in ax[row]: a.set_xlabel("slot 1"); a.set_ylabel("slot 2")242plt.tight_layout()243 244# %% cell 13 [markdown]: 4c. Interaction: wet dog245# **Reading it.** The operator is the same in both rows. What changed is **whether each expert's training data showed its object in more than one place.** So contention comes from the data: experts that never saw their object off-centre both claim the centre. In images, this predicts that cat-dog chimeras get rarer as the training data varies object position. That prediction is checkable.246#247# ### 4c. The dial is set at 0% and at 20%, and the number is the mean $x_1$ of the product's mass in the top half: $-0.8$ means the interaction was produced, and $-0.5$ means a dry dog in the rain.252 253# %% cell 14 [code]: def interaction_sets(f, n=600):254def interaction_sets(f, n=600):255    top = rng.random(n) < f256    a = np.c_[np.where(top, -0.8, -0.5) + 0.06 * rng.standard_normal(n),257              np.where(top, rng.uniform(0, 1, n), rng.uniform(-1, 0, n))]258    hid = rng.random(n) < f259    b = np.c_[np.where(hid, -0.8 + 0.06 * rng.standard_normal(n), rng.uniform(-1, 1, n)), rng.uniform(0, 1, n)]260    return a, b261 262fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 3.4))263for a_, f in zip(ax[:2], [0.0, 0.2]):264    a, b = interaction_sets(f)265    prod = density(ideal_expert(a, 0.08) + ideal_expert(b, 0.08))266    top = X2 > 0267    mean_x1 = (prod * top * X1).sum() / (prod * top).sum()268    show(a_, prod, f"product, overlap {f:.0%}\nmean x1 in top half = {mean_x1:.2f}", region=None)269a, b = interaction_sets(0.2)270ax[2].scatter(*b.T, s=3, c="tab:blue", label="B: rain (top half)")271ax[2].scatter(*a.T, s=3, c="tab:red", label="A: dog (x1=-0.5, wet x1=-0.8 in top)")272ax[2].set_xlim(-L, L); ax[2].set_ylim(-L, L); ax[2].legend(fontsize=7, loc="lower right"); ax[2].set_title("training data at 20% overlap")273plt.tight_layout()274 275# %% cell 15 [markdown]: What this notebook cannot show276# **Reading it.** At 0% overlap, neither expert has seen A under B's influence. At 20% overlap, both experts hold some shifted points, and the product lands near $-0.8$. **The product found the interaction without any extra term, once the data contained it.** This is the evidence behind `break 7`: interaction may be intersection plus a data condition, rather than a third operator.277#278# ## What this notebook cannot show279#280# - **Nothing here was sampled.** Every product is exact on the grid. A real sampler (reverse diffusion or annealed MCMC) adds its own error, and that is claim 4.281# - **The experts are ideal.** A trained network extrapolates differently from Gaussian smoothing, and on images that extrapolation is the whole hope of claim 2. These figures show what the data permits, and say nothing about what a network invents.282# - **Two dimensions only.** "Slots" and "regions" are single coordinates here. Pixels in an image are not independent coordinates, and an object's region is not fixed.
1# %% cell 1 [markdown]: What an expert learns, and the kinds of composition: worked  …2# # What an expert learns, and the kinds of composition: worked examples in 2D3#4# This notebook is the worked examples for claims 1 and 7 of [the overlap-dial idea map](IDEA_MAP.md). The definitions it illustrates are in [the composition terms](composition-terms.md).5#6# Two questions:7#8# 1. **Does expert A care how its training points are labelled?** (claim 1: the example and the break)9# 2. **Are co-occurrence, intersection, contention and interaction different things, and what produces each?** (claim 7)10#11# **No sampler appears anywhere.** In 2D, a product density can be computed exactly on a grid and normalised, so every picture below is the true target. A sampler would add its own error, which is claim 4's subject.12#13# **What an "ideal expert" is here.** A diffusion model trained to optimum on a finite training set, at noise level $\sigma$, has the score of the training points smoothed by a Gaussian:14#15# $$p^{\text{ideal}}_\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathcal{N}(x;\, x_i,\, \sigma^2 I).$$16#17# So every expert below is that formula applied to its training set, with no network trained. This is the best any trained expert can do at noise $\sigma$, which makes every failure below a property of the data or of the composition, never of training.18 19# %% cell 2 [code]: import numpy as np, torch, matplotlib.pyplot as plt20import numpy as np, torch, matplotlib.pyplot as plt21from scipy.special import logsumexp22plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "axes.titlesize": 10})23rng = np.random.default_rng(0); torch.manual_seed(0)24 25L, G = 1.1, 24126xs = np.linspace(-L, L, G)27X1, X2 = np.meshgrid(xs, xs)28grid = np.stack([X1.ravel(), X2.ravel()], 1)29cell = (xs[1] - xs[0]) ** 230TOP_LEFT = (X1 < 0) & (X2 > 0)           # the A∩B region in the quadrant setup31 32def ideal_expert(data, sigma):33    "Log-density on the grid of the training points smoothed by N(0, sigma^2 I)."34    d2 = ((grid[:, None, :] - np.asarray(data)[None]) ** 2).sum(-1)35    lp = logsumexp(-d2 / (2 * sigma**2), axis=1) - np.log(len(data)) - np.log(2 * np.pi * sigma**2)36    return lp.reshape(G, G)37 38def density(logp):39    "Normalise a log-density on the grid so it integrates to 1."40    p = np.exp(logp - logp.max()); return p / (p.sum() * cell)41 42def mass(p, region):43    return float((p * region).sum() * cell)44 45def show(ax, p, title, pts=None, region=TOP_LEFT):46    ax.imshow(p, origin="lower", extent=[-L, L, -L, L], cmap="magma")47    ax.axhline(0, color="w", lw=.4, alpha=.5); ax.axvline(0, color="w", lw=.4, alpha=.5)48    if pts is not None:49        ax.scatter(*np.asarray(pts).T, s=14, c="cyan", edgecolor="k", lw=.4)50    ax.set_title(title); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])51 52# %% cell 3 [markdown]: 1. There are two readings:103#104# - **"contains A"**: every point whose label set includes A trains $p(x\mid A)$.105# - **"exactly A"**: a point labelled {A, B} trains a separate condition {A, B}, and drops out of $p(x\mid A)$.106#107# The pool below is A's three points plus B's three points, one of which is secretly A. Version 2 labels are used throughout.108 109# %% cell 6 [code]: B_set = np.array([[0.5, 0.5], [0.6, 0.4], [-0.4, 0.6]])110B_set = np.array([[0.5, 0.5], [0.6, 0.4], [-0.4, 0.6]])111pool = np.vstack([A_set, B_set])112label_sets = [{"A"}, {"A"}, {"A", "B"}, {"B"}, {"B"}, {"A", "B"}]113 114def condition(c, scheme):115    keep = [c in s if scheme == "contains" else s == {c} for s in label_sets]116    return pool[np.array(keep)]117 118sig = 0.15119lp_all = ideal_expert(pool, sig)120fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(10, 6.6))121for row, scheme in enumerate(["contains", "exactly"]):122    dA, dB = condition("A", scheme), condition("B", scheme)123    pA_c = density(ideal_expert(dA, sig)); pB_c = density(ideal_expert(dB, sig))124    comp = density(ideal_expert(dA, sig) + ideal_expert(dB, sig) - lp_all)125    show(ax[row, 0], pA_c, f'p(x|A), "{scheme}" A: {len(dA)} points\ntop-left mass {mass(pA_c, TOP_LEFT):.2f}', dA)126    show(ax[row, 1], pB_c, f'p(x|B), "{scheme}" B: {len(dB)} points\ntop-left mass {mass(pB_c, TOP_LEFT):.2f}', dB)127    show(ax[row, 2], comp, f'composed p(x|A)p(x|B)/p(x)\ntop-left mass {mass(comp, TOP_LEFT):.2f}')128plt.tight_layout()129 130# %% cell 7 [markdown]: 3. Break, part 2: a classifier learns the hidden-B points as …131# **Reading it.** Under "contains A", the composition puts most of its mass in the top-left quadrant. Under "exactly A", the {A, B} points never train either condition, so both conditionals lose their top-left mass and the composition misses A∩B. Its leftover mass sits near the origin, between A's points and B's points, at a place no training point held. **The meaning of the condition is an axis of the experiment.** It has to be fixed and written down before the overlap dial means anything in construction (1).132#133# ## 3. Break, part 2: a classifier learns the hidden-B points as "not B"134#135# Now a classifier $p(B\mid x)$ is trained, as in classifier guidance. Its labels come from **which set a point was in**, which is the label the data actually carries. A hidden-B point in A's set is therefore labelled "not B".136#137# Each set has 400 points. 20% of A's set lies in the top half (hidden B), and 20% of B's set lies in the left half (hidden A). Guidance toward B adds $\nabla_x \log p(B\mid x)$ to the score. The arrows show the direction of that push (unit length, so only direction is drawn), and the title gives its average over the top-left quadrant: $(+1, 0)$ is straight right, $(0, +1)$ straight up.138 139# %% cell 8 [code]: def make_sets(f, n=400):140def make_sets(f, n=400):141    a = np.c_[rng.uniform(-1, 0, n), np.where(rng.random(n) < f, rng.uniform(0, 1, n), rng.uniform(-1, 0, n))]142    b = np.c_[np.where(rng.random(n) < f, rng.uniform(-1, 0, n), rng.uniform(0, 1, n)), rng.uniform(0, 1, n)]143    return a, b144 145A400, B400 = make_sets(0.2)146X = np.vstack([A400, B400])147y_from_set = np.r_[np.zeros(400), np.ones(400)]          # the label the data carries148y_true = (X[:, 1] > 0).astype(float)                       # the label the concept defines149 150def train_classifier(X, y, steps=1500):151    torch.manual_seed(0)152    net = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(2, 64), torch.nn.SiLU(), torch.nn.Linear(64, 64), torch.nn.SiLU(), torch.nn.Linear(64, 1))153    opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), 3e-3, weight_decay=1e-3)154    Xt, yt = torch.tensor(X, dtype=torch.float32), torch.tensor(y, dtype=torch.float32)[:, None]155    for _ in range(steps):156        opt.zero_grad(); torch.nn.functional.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(net(Xt), yt).backward(); opt.step()157    return net158 159fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4.2))160q = np.linspace(-0.85, 0.85, 9); Q1, Q2 = np.meshgrid(q, q)161for a, y, name in [(ax[0], y_from_set, "labels from set membership"), (ax[1], y_true, "true labels (x2 > 0)")]:162    net = train_classifier(X, y)163    with torch.no_grad():164        pB = torch.sigmoid(net(torch.tensor(grid, dtype=torch.float32))).numpy().reshape(G, G)165    qx = torch.tensor(np.c_[Q1.ravel(), Q2.ravel()], dtype=torch.float32, requires_grad=True)166    torch.nn.functional.logsigmoid(net(qx)).sum().backward()167    gr = qx.grad.numpy(); gr = gr / (np.linalg.norm(gr, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-12)168    in_tl = (qx.detach().numpy()[:, 0] < 0) & (qx.detach().numpy()[:, 1] > 0)169    push = gr[in_tl].mean(0)170    a.imshow(pB, origin="lower", extent=[-L, L, -L, L], cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=1)171    a.quiver(Q1, Q2, gr[:, 0], gr[:, 1], color="w", scale=14, width=.006)172    a.axhline(0, c="w", lw=.4); a.axvline(0, c="w", lw=.4)173    a.set_title(f"{name}\nmean p(B|x) in top-left = {pB[TOP_LEFT].mean():.2f}\nmean guidance direction there = ({push[0]:+.2f}, {push[1]:+.2f})"); a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])174plt.tight_layout()175 176# %% cell 9 [markdown]: 4a. Co-occurrence and intersection177# **Reading it.** With the labels the data carries, the classifier is unsure in the top-left quadrant, at about 0.5, because that quadrant holds equal numbers of hidden-B points labelled 0 and hidden-A points labelled 1. Its average push there is `(-0.38, -0.04)`: sideways, with almost no upward component. With the true labels it is `(-0.14, +0.99)`, straight up into B. So inside A∩B, guidance toward B has stopped meaning "more B". Its direction now follows where the label proportions happen to change (leftward toward the edge, rightward near $x_1 = 0$ into B-only), not the concept. **The classifier has learned part of "B" from where the points came from rather than from $x_2$, which is the toy's version of a shortcut**, like a pneumothorax classifier that reads the drain. With the true labels, the top-left quadrant is confidently B and the arrows point straight up.178#179# **Repaired claim 1.** A density expert learns its training set's density. Labels matter only in the parts that read them: the conditioning scheme of construction (1), and any classifier.180#181# ---182#183# ## 4. The kinds of composition, side by side184#185# Every expert below is an ideal expert built from 2,000 sampled training points. Every composition is the exact normalised product on the grid.186#187# ### 4a. Co-occurrence and intersection188#189# **Co-occurrence** (the quadrant setup): A constrains only $x_1$, B constrains only $x_2$. Each expert is broad along the other's coordinate, so the product is a product over a partition, and it lands in the top-left quadrant.190#191# **Intersection** (the notebook's ring times bar): both experts constrain both coordinates. The product keeps only where the two supports meet.192 193# %% cell 10 [code]: n = 2000194n = 2000195ring = lambda n: 0.5 * np.c_[np.cos(a := 2 * np.pi * rng.integers(0, 8, n) / 8), np.sin(a)] + 0.03 * rng.standard_normal((n, 2))196bar = lambda n: np.c_[rng.uniform(-0.2, 0.2, n), rng.uniform(-1, 1, n)]197left_half = lambda n: np.c_[rng.uniform(-1, 0, n), rng.uniform(-1, 1, n)]198top_half = lambda n: np.c_[rng.uniform(-1, 1, n), rng.uniform(0, 1, n)]199sub = lambda d: d[rng.choice(len(d), 600, replace=False)]   # subsample for speed on the grid200 201fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(10, 6.6))202for row, (fa, fb, na, nb_, region, rname) in enumerate([203        (left_half, top_half, "A: left half", "B: top half", TOP_LEFT, "top-left"),204        (ring, bar, "A: ring of 8", "B: vertical bar", (np.abs(X1) < 0.2) & (np.abs(np.hypot(X1, X2) - 0.5) < 0.1), "ring ∩ bar")]):205    lpA, lpB = ideal_expert(sub(fa(n)), 0.06), ideal_expert(sub(fb(n)), 0.06)206    show(ax[row, 0], density(lpA), na, region=None)207    show(ax[row, 1], density(lpB), nb_, region=None)208    prod = density(lpA + lpB)209    show(ax[row, 2], prod, f"product A·B\nmass in {rname} = {mass(prod, region):.2f}")210ax[0, 0].set_ylabel("co-occurrence"); ax[1, 0].set_ylabel("intersection")211plt.tight_layout()212 213# %% cell 11 [markdown]: 4b. Contention: where a chimera comes from214# ### 4b. Contention: where a chimera comes from215#216# Read the two coordinates as **two slots in an image**. A cat is the value $-0.5$ in some slot, and a dog is $+0.5$ in some slot. The other slot holds anything.217#218# - **Centred training data**: every cat image has its cat in slot 1, and so does every dog image. Both experts constrain the same slot, so the product is a product over the same variables where a partition was meant. Its mass sits at $x_1 \approx 0$, a value that is neither cat nor dog. **That is the chimera.** For Gaussians the arithmetic is exact: $\mathcal{N}(-0.5, s^2)\,\mathcal{N}(+0.5, s^2) \propto \mathcal{N}(0, s^2/2)$.219# - **Position-varied training data**: each object appears in either slot. The product now has modes at $(-0.5, +0.5)$ and $(+0.5, -0.5)$, one object per slot, both intact. **The same product operator produces co-occurrence.**220#221# The numbers: "co-occurrence" is the mass where one slot is within 0.15 of $-0.5$ and the other within 0.15 of $+0.5$. "Chimera" is the mass where neither slot is within 0.15 of either object.222 223# %% cell 12 [code]: def obj(v, n, varied):224def obj(v, n, varied):225    o = v + 0.05 * rng.standard_normal(n); other = rng.uniform(-1, 1, n)226    swap = (rng.random(n) < 0.5) if varied else np.zeros(n, bool)227    return np.where(swap[:, None], np.c_[other, o], np.c_[o, other])228 229near = lambda Z, v: np.abs(Z - v) < 0.15230CO = (near(X1, -.5) & near(X2, .5)) | (near(X1, .5) & near(X2, -.5))231CHIMERA = ~(near(X1, -.5) | near(X1, .5) | near(X2, -.5) | near(X2, .5))232 233fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(10, 6.6))234for row, varied in enumerate([False, True]):235    cat, dog = obj(-0.5, 600, varied), obj(0.5, 600, varied)236    lpc, lpd = ideal_expert(cat, 0.2), ideal_expert(dog, 0.2)237    show(ax[row, 0], density(lpc), f"cat expert ({'position-varied' if varied else 'centred'})", region=None)238    show(ax[row, 1], density(lpd), f"dog expert ({'position-varied' if varied else 'centred'})", region=None)239    prod = density(lpc + lpd)240    show(ax[row, 2], prod, f"product\nco-occurrence {mass(prod, CO):.2f} · chimera {mass(prod, CHIMERA):.2f}")241    for a in ax[row]: a.set_xlabel("slot 1"); a.set_ylabel("slot 2")242plt.tight_layout()243 244# %% cell 13 [markdown]: 4c. Interaction: wet dog245# **Reading it.** The operator is the same in both rows. What changed is **whether each expert's training data showed its object in more than one place.** So contention comes from the data: experts that never saw their object off-centre both claim the centre. In images, this predicts that cat-dog chimeras get rarer as the training data varies object position. That prediction is checkable.246#247# ### 4c. Interaction: wet dog248#249# B is rain: the top half, with any $x_1$. A is a dog. Inside the A∩B quadrant, A looks different: its $x_1$ shifts from $-0.5$ to $-0.8$ when B is present (the dog is wet). Everywhere else A sits at $x_1 \approx -0.5$.250#251# Separately trained experts see the shifted version only through the overlap in their training sets. The dial is set at 0% and at 20%, and the number is the mean $x_1$ of the product's mass in the top half: $-0.8$ means the interaction was produced, and $-0.5$ means a dry dog in the rain.252 253# %% cell 14 [code]: def interaction_sets(f, n=600):254def interaction_sets(f, n=600):255    top = rng.random(n) < f256    a = np.c_[np.where(top, -0.8, -0.5) + 0.06 * rng.standard_normal(n),257              np.where(top, rng.uniform(0, 1, n), rng.uniform(-1, 0, n))]258    hid = rng.random(n) < f259    b = np.c_[np.where(hid, -0.8 + 0.06 * rng.standard_normal(n), rng.uniform(-1, 1, n)), rng.uniform(0, 1, n)]260    return a, b261 262fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 3.4))263for a_, f in zip(ax[:2], [0.0, 0.2]):264    a, b = interaction_sets(f)265    prod = density(ideal_expert(a, 0.08) + ideal_expert(b, 0.08))266    top = X2 > 0267    mean_x1 = (prod * top * X1).sum() / (prod * top).sum()268    show(a_, prod, f"product, overlap {f:.0%}\nmean x1 in top half = {mean_x1:.2f}", region=None)269a, b = interaction_sets(0.2)270ax[2].scatter(*b.T, s=3, c="tab:blue", label="B: rain (top half)")271ax[2].scatter(*a.T, s=3, c="tab:red", label="A: dog (x1=-0.5, wet x1=-0.8 in top)")272ax[2].set_xlim(-L, L); ax[2].set_ylim(-L, L); ax[2].legend(fontsize=7, loc="lower right"); ax[2].set_title("training data at 20% overlap")273plt.tight_layout()274 275# %% cell 15 [markdown]: What this notebook cannot show276# **Reading it.** At 0% overlap, neither expert has seen A under B's influence. The product puts its top-half mass near $x_1 = -0.5$, hugging the boundary $x_2 \approx 0$ where the dog expert's smoothed tail meets the rain: a dry dog at the edge of the rain. At 20% overlap, both experts hold some shifted points, and the product lands near $-0.8$. **The product found the interaction without any extra term, once the data contained it.** This is the evidence behind `break 7`: interaction may be intersection plus a data condition, rather than a third operator.277#278# ## What this notebook cannot show279#280# - **Nothing here was sampled.** Every product is exact on the grid. A real sampler (reverse diffusion or annealed MCMC) adds its own error, and that is claim 4.281# - **The experts are ideal.** A trained network extrapolates differently from Gaussian smoothing, and on images that extrapolation is the whole hope of claim 2. These figures show what the data permits, and say nothing about what a network invents.282# - **Two dimensions only.** "Slots" and "regions" are single coordinates here. Pixels in an image are not independent coordinates, and an object's region is not fixed.
1# %% cell 1 [markdown]: What an expert learns, and the kinds of composition: worked  …2# # What an expert learns, and the kinds of composition: worked examples in 2D3#4# This notebook is the worked examples for claims 1 and 7 of [the overlap-dial idea map](IDEA_MAP.md). The definitions it illustrates are in [the composition terms](composition-terms.md).5#6# Two questions:7#8# 1. **Does expert A care how its training points are labelled?** (claim 1: the example and the break)9# 2. **Are co-occurrence, intersection, contention and interaction different things, and what produces each?** (claim 7)10#11# **No sampler appears anywhere.** In 2D, a product density can be computed exactly on a grid and normalised, so every picture below is the true target. A sampler would add its own error, which is claim 4's subject.12#13# **What an "ideal expert" is here.** A diffusion model trained to optimum on a finite training set, at noise level $\sigma$, has the score of the training points smoothed by a Gaussian:14#15# $$p^{\text{ideal}}_\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathcal{N}(x;\, x_i,\, \sigma^2 I).$$16#17# So every expert below is that formula applied to its training set, with no network trained. This is the best any trained expert can do at noise $\sigma$, which makes every failure below a property of the data or of the composition, never of training.18 19# %% cell 2 [code]: import numpy as np, torch, matplotlib.pyplot as plt20import numpy as np, torch, matplotlib.pyplot as plt21from scipy.special import logsumexp22plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "axes.titlesize": 10})23rng = np.random.default_rng(0); torch.manual_seed(0)24 25L, G = 1.1, 24126xs = np.linspace(-L, L, G)27X1, X2 = np.meshgrid(xs, xs)28grid = np.stack([X1.ravel(), X2.ravel()], 1)29cell = (xs[1] - xs[0]) ** 230TOP_LEFT = (X1 < 0) & (X2 > 0)           # the A∩B region in the quadrant setup31 32def ideal_expert(data, sigma):33    "Log-density on the grid of the training points smoothed by N(0, sigma^2 I)."34    d2 = ((grid[:, None, :] - np.asarray(data)[None]) ** 2).sum(-1)35    lp = logsumexp(-d2 / (2 * sigma**2), axis=1) - np.log(len(data)) - np.log(2 * np.pi * sigma**2)36    return lp.reshape(G, G)37 38def density(logp):39    "Normalise a log-density on the grid so it integrates to 1."40    p = np.exp(logp - logp.max()); return p / (p.sum() * cell)41 42def mass(p, region):43    return float((p * region).sum() * cell)44 45def show(ax, p, title, pts=None, region=TOP_LEFT):46    ax.imshow(p, origin="lower", extent=[-L, L, -L, L], cmap="magma")47    ax.axhline(0, color="w", lw=.4, alpha=.5); ax.axvline(0, color="w", lw=.4, alpha=.5)48    if pts is not None:49        ax.scatter(*np.asarray(pts).T, s=14, c="cyan", edgecolor="k", lw=.4)50    ax.set_title(title); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])51 52# %% cell 3 [markdown]: 1. Example: same points, different labels, same expert53# ## 1. Example: same points, different labels, same expert54#55# Expert A's training set is three points. In **version 1** all three are labelled "A", and the top-left one is secretly also B. In **version 2** the top-left one is labelled "A, B".56#57# The denoising loss expert A minimises is58#59# $$\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{x_0 \sim \text{A's set},\ t,\ \varepsilon}\ \big\| \varepsilon - \varepsilon_\theta(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\varepsilon,\ t) \big\|^2 .$$60#61# **No label appears in it.** The only thing a label could change is which points are in A's set, and here it changes nothing.62 63# %% cell 4 [code]: A_set = np.array([[-0.5, -0.5], [-0.6, -0.4], [-0.5, 0.5]])64A_set = np.array([[-0.5, -0.5], [-0.6, -0.4], [-0.5, 0.5]])65labels_v1 = ["A", "A", "A (secretly B)"]66labels_v2 = ["A", "A", "A, B"]67 68# a tiny denoiser, one gradient step on each version, same seed: the labels are never an input69def one_step_grads(x0):70    torch.manual_seed(1)71    net = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(3, 32), torch.nn.SiLU(), torch.nn.Linear(32, 2))72    x0 = torch.tensor(x0, dtype=torch.float32).repeat(64, 1)73    t = torch.rand(len(x0), 1); abar = torch.cos(t * torch.pi / 2) ** 274    eps = torch.randn_like(x0)75    xt = abar.sqrt() * x0 + (1 - abar).sqrt() * eps76    loss = ((eps - net(torch.cat([xt, t], 1))) ** 2).mean()77    loss.backward()78    return torch.cat([p.grad.flatten() for p in net.parameters()])79 80g1, g2 = one_step_grads(A_set), one_step_grads(A_set)   # version 1 and version 2 feed the same x081print("largest difference between the two versions' gradients:", (g1 - g2).abs().max().item())82 83pA = density(ideal_expert(A_set, sigma=0.15))84fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 3.4))85for a, labs, name in [(ax[0], labels_v1, "version 1 labels"), (ax[1], labels_v2, "version 2 labels")]:86    a.scatter(*A_set.T, s=40, c="tab:red"); a.set_xlim(-L, L); a.set_ylim(-L, L)87    a.axhline(0, c="grey", lw=.5); a.axvline(0, c="grey", lw=.5)88    for (x, y), s in zip(A_set, labs): a.annotate(s, (x, y), (5, 5), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=8)89    a.set_title(name); a.set_aspect("equal")90show(ax[2], pA, f"expert A, both versions\nmass in top-left (A∩B) = {mass(pA, TOP_LEFT):.2f}", A_set)91plt.tight_layout()92 93# %% cell 5 [markdown]: 2. The arrows show the direction of that push (unit length, so only direction is drawn), and the title gives its average over the top-left quadrant: $(+1, 0)$ is straight right, $(0, +1)$ straight up.138 139# %% cell 8 [code]: def make_sets(f, n=400):140def make_sets(f, n=400):141    a = np.c_[rng.uniform(-1, 0, n), np.where(rng.random(n) < f, rng.uniform(0, 1, n), rng.uniform(-1, 0, n))]142    b = np.c_[np.where(rng.random(n) < f, rng.uniform(-1, 0, n), rng.uniform(0, 1, n)), rng.uniform(0, 1, n)]143    return a, b144 145A400, B400 = make_sets(0.2)146X = np.vstack([A400, B400])147y_from_set = np.r_[np.zeros(400), np.ones(400)]          # the label the data carries148y_true = (X[:, 1] > 0).astype(float)                       # the label the concept defines149 150def train_classifier(X, y, steps=1500):151    torch.manual_seed(0)152    net = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(2, 64), torch.nn.SiLU(), torch.nn.Linear(64, 64), torch.nn.SiLU(), torch.nn.Linear(64, 1))153    opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), 3e-3, weight_decay=1e-3)154    Xt, yt = torch.tensor(X, dtype=torch.float32), torch.tensor(y, dtype=torch.float32)[:, None]155    for _ in range(steps):156        opt.zero_grad(); torch.nn.functional.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(net(Xt), yt).backward(); opt.step()157    return net158 159fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4.2))160q = np.linspace(-0.85, 0.85, 9); Q1, Q2 = np.meshgrid(q, q)161for a, y, name in [(ax[0], y_from_set, "labels from set membership"), (ax[1], y_true, "true labels (x2 > 0)")]:162    net = train_classifier(X, y)163    with torch.no_grad():164        pB = torch.sigmoid(net(torch.tensor(grid, dtype=torch.float32))).numpy().reshape(G, G)165    qx = torch.tensor(np.c_[Q1.ravel(), Q2.ravel()], dtype=torch.float32, requires_grad=True)166    torch.nn.functional.logsigmoid(net(qx)).sum().backward()167    gr = qx.grad.numpy(); gr = gr / (np.linalg.norm(gr, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-12)168    in_tl = (qx.detach().numpy()[:, 0] < 0) & (qx.detach().numpy()[:, 1] > 0)169    push = gr[in_tl].mean(0)170    a.imshow(pB, origin="lower", extent=[-L, L, -L, L], cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=1)171    a.quiver(Q1, Q2, gr[:, 0], gr[:, 1], color="w", scale=14, width=.006)172    a.axhline(0, c="w", lw=.4); a.axvline(0, c="w", lw=.4)173    a.set_title(f"{name}\nmean p(B|x) in top-left = {pB[TOP_LEFT].mean():.2f}\nmean guidance direction there = ({push[0]:+.2f}, {push[1]:+.2f})"); a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])174plt.tight_layout()175 176# %% cell 9 [markdown]: 4a. Co-occurrence and intersection177# **Reading it.** With the labels the data carries, the classifier is unsure in the top-left quadrant, at about 0.5, because that quadrant holds equal numbers of hidden-B points labelled 0 and hidden-A points labelled 1. Its average push there is `(-0.38, -0.04)`: sideways, with almost no upward component. With the true labels it is `(-0.14, +0.99)`, straight up into B. So inside A∩B, guidance toward B has stopped meaning "more B". Its direction now follows where the label proportions happen to change (leftward toward the edge, rightward near $x_1 = 0$ into B-only), not the concept. **The classifier has learned part of "B" from where the points came from rather than from $x_2$, which is the toy's version of a shortcut**, like a pneumothorax classifier that reads the drain. With the true labels, the top-left quadrant is confidently B and the arrows point straight up.178#179# **Repaired claim 1.** A density expert learns its training set's density. Labels matter only in the parts that read them: the conditioning scheme of construction (1), and any classifier.180#181# ---182#183# ## 4. The kinds of composition, side by side184#185# Every expert below is an ideal expert built from 2,000 sampled training points. Co-occurrence and intersection188#189# **Co-occurrence** (the quadrant setup): A constrains only $x_1$, B constrains only $x_2$. The product keeps only where the two supports meet.192 193# %% cell 10 [code]: n = 2000194n = 2000195ring = lambda n: 0.5 * np.c_[np.cos(a := 2 * np.pi * rng.integers(0, 8, n) / 8), np.sin(a)] + 0.03 * rng.standard_normal((n, 2))196bar = lambda n: np.c_[rng.uniform(-0.2, 0.2, n), rng.uniform(-1, 1, n)]197left_half = lambda n: np.c_[rng.uniform(-1, 0, n), rng.uniform(-1, 1, n)]198top_half = lambda n: np.c_[rng.uniform(-1, 1, n), rng.uniform(0, 1, n)]199sub = lambda d: d[rng.choice(len(d), 600, replace=False)]   # subsample for speed on the grid200 201fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(10, 6.6))202for row, (fa, fb, na, nb_, region, rname) in enumerate([203        (left_half, top_half, "A: left half", "B: top half", TOP_LEFT, "top-left"),204        (ring, bar, "A: ring of 8", "B: vertical bar", (np.abs(X1) < 0.2) & (np.abs(np.hypot(X1, X2) - 0.5) < 0.1), "ring ∩ bar")]):205    lpA, lpB = ideal_expert(sub(fa(n)), 0.06), ideal_expert(sub(fb(n)), 0.06)206    show(ax[row, 0], density(lpA), na, region=None)207    show(ax[row, 1], density(lpB), nb_, region=None)208    prod = density(lpA + lpB)209    show(ax[row, 2], prod, f"product A·B\nmass in {rname} = {mass(prod, region):.2f}")210ax[0, 0].set_ylabel("co-occurrence"); ax[1, 0].set_ylabel("intersection")211plt.tight_layout()212 213# %% cell 11 [markdown]: 4b. Contention: where a chimera comes from214# ### 4b. Contention: where a chimera comes from215#216# Read the two coordinates as **two slots in an image**. A cat is the value $-0.5$ in some slot, and a dog is $+0.5$ in some slot. The other slot holds anything.217#218# - **Centred training data**: every cat image has its cat in slot 1, and so does every dog image. Both experts constrain the same slot, so the product is a product over the same variables where a partition was meant. Its mass sits at $x_1 \approx 0$, a value that is neither cat nor dog. **That is the chimera.** For Gaussians the arithmetic is exact: $\mathcal{N}(-0.5, s^2)\,\mathcal{N}(+0.5, s^2) \propto \mathcal{N}(0, s^2/2)$.219# - **Position-varied training data**: each object appears in either slot. The product now has modes at $(-0.5, +0.5)$ and $(+0.5, -0.5)$, one object per slot, both intact. **The same product operator produces co-occurrence.**220#221# The numbers: "co-occurrence" is the mass where one slot is within 0.15 of $-0.5$ and the other within 0.15 of $+0.5$. "Chimera" is the mass where neither slot is within 0.15 of either object.222 223# %% cell 12 [code]: def obj(v, n, varied):224def obj(v, n, varied):225    o = v + 0.05 * rng.standard_normal(n); other = rng.uniform(-1, 1, n)226    swap = (rng.random(n) < 0.5) if varied else np.zeros(n, bool)227    return np.where(swap[:, None], np.c_[other, o], np.c_[o, other])228 229near = lambda Z, v: np.abs(Z - v) < 0.15230CO = (near(X1, -.5) & near(X2, .5)) | (near(X1, .5) & near(X2, -.5))231CHIMERA = ~(near(X1, -.5) | near(X1, .5) | near(X2, -.5) | near(X2, .5))232 233fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(10, 6.6))234for row, varied in enumerate([False, True]):235    cat, dog = obj(-0.5, 600, varied), obj(0.5, 600, varied)236    lpc, lpd = ideal_expert(cat, 0.2), ideal_expert(dog, 0.2)237    show(ax[row, 0], density(lpc), f"cat expert ({'position-varied' if varied else 'centred'})", region=None)238    show(ax[row, 1], density(lpd), f"dog expert ({'position-varied' if varied else 'centred'})", region=None)239    prod = density(lpc + lpd)240    show(ax[row, 2], prod, f"product\nco-occurrence {mass(prod, CO):.2f} · chimera {mass(prod, CHIMERA):.2f}")241    for a in ax[row]: a.set_xlabel("slot 1"); a.set_ylabel("slot 2")242plt.tight_layout()243 244# %% cell 13 [markdown]: 4c. Interaction: wet dog245# **Reading it.** The operator is the same in both rows. What changed is **whether each expert's training data showed its object in more than one place.** So contention comes from the data: experts that never saw their object off-centre both claim the centre. In images, this predicts that cat-dog chimeras get rarer as the training data varies object position. That prediction is checkable.246#247# ### 4c. Interaction: wet dog248#249# B is rain: the top half, with any $x_1$. A is a dog. Inside the A∩B quadrant, A looks different: its $x_1$ shifts from $-0.5$ to $-0.8$ when B is present (the dog is wet). Everywhere else A sits at $x_1 \approx -0.5$.250#251# Separately trained experts see the shifted version only through the overlap in their training sets. The dial is set at 0% and at 20%, and the number is the mean $x_1$ of the product's mass in the top half: $-0.8$ means the interaction was produced, and $-0.5$ means a dry dog in the rain.252 253# %% cell 14 [code]: def interaction_sets(f, n=600):254def interaction_sets(f, n=600):255    top = rng.random(n) < f256    a = np.c_[np.where(top, -0.8, -0.5) + 0.06 * rng.standard_normal(n),257              np.where(top, rng.uniform(0, 1, n), rng.uniform(-1, 0, n))]258    hid = rng.random(n) < f259    b = np.c_[np.where(hid, -0.8 + 0.06 * rng.standard_normal(n), rng.uniform(-1, 1, n)), rng.uniform(0, 1, n)]260    return a, b261 262fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 3.4))263for a_, f in zip(ax[:2], [0.0, 0.2]):264    a, b = interaction_sets(f)265    prod = density(ideal_expert(a, 0.08) + ideal_expert(b, 0.08))266    top = X2 > 0267    mean_x1 = (prod * top * X1).sum() / (prod * top).sum()268    show(a_, prod, f"product, overlap {f:.0%}\nmean x1 in top half = {mean_x1:.2f}", region=None)269a, b = interaction_sets(0.2)270ax[2].scatter(*b.T, s=3, c="tab:blue", label="B: rain (top half)")271ax[2].scatter(*a.T, s=3, c="tab:red", label="A: dog (x1=-0.5, wet x1=-0.8 in top)")272ax[2].set_xlim(-L, L); ax[2].set_ylim(-L, L); ax[2].legend(fontsize=7, loc="lower right"); ax[2].set_title("training data at 20% overlap")273plt.tight_layout()274 275# %% cell 15 [markdown]: What this notebook cannot show276# **Reading it.** At 0% overlap, neither expert has seen A under B's influence. 1# %% cell 1 [markdown]: What an expert learns, and the kinds of composition: worked  …2# # What an expert learns, and the kinds of composition: worked examples in 2D3#4# This notebook is the worked examples for claims 1 and 7 of [the overlap-dial idea map](IDEA_MAP.md). The definitions it illustrates are in [the composition terms](composition-terms.md).5#6# Two questions:7#8# 1. **Does expert A care how its training points are labelled?** (claim 1: the example and the break)9# 2. **Are co-occurrence, intersection, contention and interaction different things, and what produces each?** (claim 7)10#11# **No sampler appears anywhere.** In 2D, a product density can be computed exactly on a grid and normalised, so every picture below is the true target. A sampler would add its own error, which is claim 4's subject.12#13# **What an "ideal expert" is here.** A diffusion model trained to optimum on a finite training set, at noise level $\sigma$, has the score of the training points smoothed by a Gaussian:14#15# $$p^{\text{ideal}}_\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathcal{N}(x;\, x_i,\, \sigma^2 I).$$16#17# So every expert below is that formula applied to its training set, with no network trained. This is the best any trained expert can do at noise $\sigma$, which makes every failure below a property of the data or of the composition, never of training.18 19# %% cell 2 [code]: import numpy as np, torch, matplotlib.pyplot as plt20import numpy as np, torch, matplotlib.pyplot as plt21from scipy.special import logsumexp22plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "axes.titlesize": 10})23rng = np.random.default_rng(0); torch.manual_seed(0)24 25L, G = 1.1, 24126xs = np.linspace(-L, L, G)27X1, X2 = np.meshgrid(xs, xs)28grid = np.stack([X1.ravel(), X2.ravel()], 1)29cell = (xs[1] - xs[0]) ** 230TOP_LEFT = (X1 < 0) & (X2 > 0)           # the A∩B region in the quadrant setup31 32def ideal_expert(data, sigma):33    "Log-density on the grid of the training points smoothed by N(0, sigma^2 I)."34    d2 = ((grid[:, None, :] - np.asarray(data)[None]) ** 2).sum(-1)35    lp = logsumexp(-d2 / (2 * sigma**2), axis=1) - np.log(len(data)) - np.log(2 * np.pi * sigma**2)36    return lp.reshape(G, G)37 38def density(logp):39    "Normalise a log-density on the grid so it integrates to 1."40    p = np.exp(logp - logp.max()); return p / (p.sum() * cell)41 42def mass(p, region):43    return float((p * region).sum() * cell)44 45def show(ax, p, title, pts=None, region=TOP_LEFT):46    ax.imshow(p, origin="lower", extent=[-L, L, -L, L], cmap="magma")47    ax.axhline(0, color="w", lw=.4, alpha=.5); ax.axvline(0, color="w", lw=.4, alpha=.5)48    if pts is not None:49        ax.scatter(*np.asarray(pts).T, s=14, c="cyan", edgecolor="k", lw=.4)50    ax.set_title(title); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])51 52# %% cell 3 [markdown]: 1. In **version 1** all three are labelled "A", and the top-left one is secretly also B. In **version 2** the top-left one is labelled "A, B".56#57# The denoising loss expert A minimises is58#59# $$\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{x_0 \sim \text{A's set},\ t,\ \varepsilon}\ \big\| \varepsilon - \varepsilon_\theta(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\varepsilon,\ t) \big\|^2 .$$60#61# **No label appears in it.** The only thing a label could change is which points are in A's set, and here it changes nothing.62 63# %% cell 4 [code]: A_set = np.array([[-0.5, -0.5], [-0.6, -0.4], [-0.5, 0.5]])64A_set = np.array([[-0.5, -0.5], [-0.6, -0.4], [-0.5, 0.5]])65labels_v1 = ["A", "A", "A (secretly B)"]66labels_v2 = ["A", "A", "A, B"]67 68# a tiny denoiser, one gradient step on each version, same seed: the labels are never an input69def one_step_grads(x0):70    torch.manual_seed(1)71    net = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(3, 32), torch.nn.SiLU(), torch.nn.Linear(32, 2))72    x0 = torch.tensor(x0, dtype=torch.float32).repeat(64, 1)73    t = torch.rand(len(x0), 1); abar = torch.cos(t * torch.pi / 2) ** 274    eps = torch.randn_like(x0)75    xt = abar.sqrt() * x0 + (1 - abar).sqrt() * eps76    loss = ((eps - net(torch.cat([xt, t], 1))) ** 2).mean()77    loss.backward()78    return torch.cat([p.grad.flatten() for p in net.parameters()])79 80g1, g2 = one_step_grads(A_set), one_step_grads(A_set)   # version 1 and version 2 feed the same x081print("largest difference between the two versions' gradients:", (g1 - g2).abs().max().item())82 83pA = density(ideal_expert(A_set, sigma=0.15))84fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 3.4))85for a, labs, name in [(ax[0], labels_v1, "version 1 labels"), (ax[1], labels_v2, "version 2 labels")]:86    a.scatter(*A_set.T, s=40, c="tab:red"); Break, part 1: labels matter to a conditional model (construction 1)97#98# Construction (1) trains one model on everything, conditioned on a label, and composes99#100# $$\nabla \log p(x\mid A) + \nabla \log p(x\mid B) - \nabla \log p(x) \;=\; \nabla \log \frac{p(x\mid A)\,p(x\mid B)}{p(x)} .$$101#102# Now the label decides which points train the condition "A". Contention: where a chimera comes from214# ### 4b. Contention: where a chimera comes from215#216# Read the two coordinates as **two slots in an image**. The other slot holds anything.217#218# - **Centred training data**: every cat image has its cat in slot 1, and so does every dog image. Both experts constrain the same slot, so the product is a product over the same variables where a partition was meant. Its mass sits at $x_1 \approx 0$, a value that is neither cat nor dog. **That is the chimera.** For Gaussians the arithmetic is exact: $\mathcal{N}(-0.5, s^2)\,\mathcal{N}(+0.5, s^2) \propto \mathcal{N}(0, s^2/2)$.219# - **Position-varied training data**: each object appears in either slot. "Chimera" is the mass where neither slot is within 0.15 of either object.222 223# %% cell 12 [code]: def obj(v, n, varied):224def obj(v, n, varied):225    o = v + 0.05 * rng.standard_normal(n); other = rng.uniform(-1, 1, n)226    swap = (rng.random(n) < 0.5) if varied else np.zeros(n, bool)227    return np.where(swap[:, None], np.c_[other, o], np.c_[o, other])228 229near = lambda Z, v: np.abs(Z - v) < 0.15230CO = (near(X1, -.5) & near(X2, .5)) | (near(X1, .5) & near(X2, -.5))231CHIMERA = ~(near(X1, -.5) | near(X1, .5) | near(X2, -.5) | near(X2, .5))232 233fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(10, 6.6))234for row, varied in enumerate([False, True]):235    cat, dog = obj(-0.5, 600, varied), obj(0.5, 600, varied)236    lpc, lpd = ideal_expert(cat, 0.2), ideal_expert(dog, 0.2)237    show(ax[row, 0], density(lpc), f"cat expert ({'position-varied' if varied else 'centred'})", region=None)238    show(ax[row, 1], density(lpd), f"dog expert ({'position-varied' if varied else 'centred'})", region=None)239    prod = density(lpc + lpd)240    show(ax[row, 2], prod, f"product\nco-occurrence {mass(prod, CO):.2f} · chimera {mass(prod, CHIMERA):.2f}")241    for a in ax[row]: a.set_xlabel("slot 1"); a.set_ylabel("slot 2")242plt.tight_layout()243 244# %% cell 13 [markdown]: 4c. Interaction: wet dog245# **Reading it.** The operator is the same in both rows. What changed is **whether each expert's training data showed its object in more than one place.** So contention comes from the data: experts that never saw their object off-centre both claim the centre. Everywhere else A sits at $x_1 \approx -0.5$.250#251# Separately trained experts see the shifted version only through the overlap in their training sets. The dial is set at 0% and at 20%, and the number is the mean $x_1$ of the product's mass in the top half: $-0.8$ means the interaction was produced, and $-0.5$ means a dry dog in the rain.252 253# %% cell 14 [code]: def interaction_sets(f, n=600):254def interaction_sets(f, n=600):255    top = rng.random(n) < f256    a = np.c_[np.where(top, -0.8, -0.5) + 0.06 * rng.standard_normal(n),257              np.where(top, rng.uniform(0, 1, n), rng.uniform(-1, 0, n))]258    hid = rng.random(n) < f259    b = np.c_[np.where(hid, -0.8 + 0.06 * rng.standard_normal(n), rng.uniform(-1, 1, n)), rng.uniform(0, 1, n)]260    return a, b261 262fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 3.4))263for a_, f in zip(ax[:2], [0.0, 0.2]):264    a, b = interaction_sets(f)265    prod = density(ideal_expert(a, 0.08) + ideal_expert(b, 0.08))266    top = X2 > 0267    mean_x1 = (prod * top * X1).sum() / (prod * top).sum()268    show(a_, prod, f"product, overlap {f:.0%}\nmean x1 in top half = {mean_x1:.2f}", region=None)269a, b = interaction_sets(0.2)270ax[2].scatter(*b.T, s=3, c="tab:blue", label="B: rain (top half)")271ax[2].scatter(*a.T, s=3, c="tab:red", label="A: dog (x1=-0.5, wet x1=-0.8 in top)")272ax[2].set_xlim(-L, L); ax[2].set_ylim(-L, L); ax[2].legend(fontsize=7, loc="lower right"); ax[2].set_title("training data at 20% overlap")273plt.tight_layout()274 275# %% cell 15 [markdown]: What this notebook cannot show276# **Reading it.** At 0% overlap, neither expert has seen A under B's influence. 1# %% cell 1 [markdown]: What an expert learns, and the kinds of composition: worked  …2# # What an expert learns, and the kinds of composition: worked examples in 2D3#4# This notebook is the worked examples for claims 1 and 7 of [the overlap-dial idea map](IDEA_MAP.md). The definitions it illustrates are in [the composition terms](composition-terms.md).5#6# Two questions:7#8# 1. **Does expert A care how its training points are labelled?** (claim 1: the example and the break)9# 2. **Are co-occurrence, intersection, contention and interaction different things, and what produces each?** (claim 7)10#11# **No sampler appears anywhere.** In 2D, a product density can be computed exactly on a grid and normalised, so every picture below is the true target. A sampler would add its own error, which is claim 4's subject.12#13# **What an "ideal expert" is here.** A diffusion model trained to optimum on a finite training set, at noise level $\sigma$, has the score of the training points smoothed by a Gaussian:14#15# $$p^{\text{ideal}}_\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathcal{N}(x;\, x_i,\, \sigma^2 I).$$16#17# So every expert below is that formula applied to its training set, with no network trained. This is the best any trained expert can do at noise $\sigma$, which makes every failure below a property of the data or of the composition, never of training.18 19# %% cell 2 [code]: import numpy as np, torch, matplotlib.pyplot as plt20import numpy as np, torch, matplotlib.pyplot as plt21from scipy.special import logsumexp22plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "axes.titlesize": 10})23rng = np.random.default_rng(0); torch.manual_seed(0)24 25L, G = 1.1, 24126xs = np.linspace(-L, L, G)27X1, X2 = np.meshgrid(xs, xs)28grid = np.stack([X1.ravel(), X2.ravel()], 1)29cell = (xs[1] - xs[0]) ** 230TOP_LEFT = (X1 < 0) & (X2 > 0)           # the A∩B region in the quadrant setup31 32def ideal_expert(data, sigma):33    "Log-density on the grid of the training points smoothed by N(0, sigma^2 I)."34    d2 = ((grid[:, None, :] - np.asarray(data)[None]) ** 2).sum(-1)35    lp = logsumexp(-d2 / (2 * sigma**2), axis=1) - np.log(len(data)) - np.log(2 * np.pi * sigma**2)36    return lp.reshape(G, G)37 38def density(logp):39    "Normalise a log-density on the grid so it integrates to 1."40    p = np.exp(logp - logp.max()); return p / (p.sum() * cell)41 42def mass(p, region):43    return float((p * region).sum() * cell)44 45def show(ax, p, title, pts=None, region=TOP_LEFT):46    ax.imshow(p, origin="lower", extent=[-L, L, -L, L], cmap="magma")47    ax.axhline(0, color="w", lw=.4, alpha=.5); ax.axvline(0, color="w", lw=.4, alpha=.5)48    if pts is not None:49        ax.scatter(*np.asarray(pts).T, s=14, c="cyan", edgecolor="k", lw=.4)50    ax.set_title(title); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])51 52# %% cell 3 [markdown]: 1. Example: same points, different labels, same expert53# ## 1. Example: same points, different labels, same expert54#55# Expert A's training set is three points. In **version 1** all three are labelled "A", and the top-left one is secretly also B. In **version 2** the top-left one is labelled "A, B".56#57# The denoising loss expert A minimises is58#59# $$\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{x_0 \sim \text{A's set},\ t,\ \varepsilon}\ \big\| \varepsilon - \varepsilon_\theta(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\varepsilon,\ t) \big\|^2 .$$60#61# **No label appears in it.** The only thing a label could change is which points are in A's set, and here it changes nothing.62 63# %% cell 4 [code]: A_set = np.array([[-0.5, -0.5], [-0.6, -0.4], [-0.5, 0.5]])64A_set = np.array([[-0.5, -0.5], [-0.6, -0.4], [-0.5, 0.5]])65labels_v1 = ["A", "A", "A (secretly B)"]66labels_v2 = ["A", "A", "A, B"]67 68# a tiny denoiser, one gradient step on each version, same seed: the labels are never an input69def one_step_grads(x0):70    torch.manual_seed(1)71    net = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(3, 32), torch.nn.SiLU(), torch.nn.Linear(32, 2))72    x0 = torch.tensor(x0, dtype=torch.float32).repeat(64, 1)73    t = torch.rand(len(x0), 1); abar = torch.cos(t * torch.pi / 2) ** 274    eps = torch.randn_like(x0)75    xt = abar.sqrt() * x0 + (1 - abar).sqrt() * eps76    loss = ((eps - net(torch.cat([xt, t], 1))) ** 2).mean()77    loss.backward()78    return torch.cat([p.grad.flatten() for p in net.parameters()])79 80g1, g2 = one_step_grads(A_set), one_step_grads(A_set)   # version 1 and version 2 feed the same x081print("largest difference between the two versions' gradients:", (g1 - g2).abs().max().item())82 83pA = density(ideal_expert(A_set, sigma=0.15))84fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 3.4))85for a, labs, name in [(ax[0], labels_v1, "version 1 labels"), (ax[1], labels_v2, "version 2 labels")]:86    a.scatter(*A_set.T, s=40, c="tab:red"); a.set_xlim(-L, L); a.set_ylim(-L, L)87    a.axhline(0, c="grey", lw=.5); a.axvline(0, c="grey", lw=.5)88    for (x, y), s in zip(A_set, labs): a.annotate(s, (x, y), (5, 5), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=8)89    a.set_title(name); a.set_aspect("equal")90show(ax[2], pA, f"expert A, both versions\nmass in top-left (A∩B) = {mass(pA, TOP_LEFT):.2f}", A_set)91plt.tight_layout()92 93# %% cell 5 [markdown]: 2. Break, part 1: labels matter to a conditional model (cons …94# **Reading it.** The gradient difference is exactly `0.0`, and the one heatmap serves both versions. A third of expert A's mass sits in the top-left quadrant, because one of its three points is there. **For separately trained experts (construction 2), "hidden B" and "labelled A and B" are the same experiment.**95#96# ## 2. Break, part 1: labels matter to a conditional model (construction 1)97#98# Construction (1) trains one model on everything, conditioned on a label, and composes99#100# $$\nabla \log p(x\mid A) + \nabla \log p(x\mid B) - \nabla \log p(x) \;=\; \nabla \log \frac{p(x\mid A)\,p(x\mid B)}{p(x)} .$$101#102# Now the label decides which points train the condition "A". There are two readings:103#104# - **"contains A"**: every point whose label set includes A trains $p(x\mid A)$.105# - **"exactly A"**: a point labelled {A, B} trains a separate condition {A, B}, and drops out of $p(x\mid A)$.106#107# The pool below is A's three points plus B's three points, one of which is secretly A. Version 2 labels are used throughout.108 109# %% cell 6 [code]: B_set = np.array([[0.5, 0.5], [0.6, 0.4], [-0.4, 0.6]])110B_set = np.array([[0.5, 0.5], [0.6, 0.4], [-0.4, 0.6]])111pool = np.vstack([A_set, B_set])112label_sets = [{"A"}, {"A"}, {"A", "B"}, {"B"}, {"B"}, {"A", "B"}]113 114def condition(c, scheme):115    keep = [c in s if scheme == "contains" else s == {c} for s in label_sets]116    return pool[np.array(keep)]117 118sig = 0.15119lp_all = ideal_expert(pool, sig)120fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(10, 6.6))121for row, scheme in enumerate(["contains", "exactly"]):122    dA, dB = condition("A", scheme), condition("B", scheme)123    pA_c = density(ideal_expert(dA, sig)); pB_c = density(ideal_expert(dB, sig))124    comp = density(ideal_expert(dA, sig) + ideal_expert(dB, sig) - lp_all)125    show(ax[row, 0], pA_c, f'p(x|A), "{scheme}" A: {len(dA)} points\ntop-left mass {mass(pA_c, TOP_LEFT):.2f}', dA)126    show(ax[row, 1], pB_c, f'p(x|B), "{scheme}" B: {len(dB)} points\ntop-left mass {mass(pB_c, TOP_LEFT):.2f}', dB)127    show(ax[row, 2], comp, f'composed p(x|A)p(x|B)/p(x)\ntop-left mass {mass(comp, TOP_LEFT):.2f}')128plt.tight_layout()129 130# %% cell 7 [markdown]: 3. The arrows show the direction of that push (unit length, so only direction is drawn), and the title gives its average over the top-left quadrant: $(+1, 0)$ is straight right, $(0, +1)$ straight up.138 139# %% cell 8 [code]: def make_sets(f, n=400):140def make_sets(f, n=400):141    a = np.c_[rng.uniform(-1, 0, n), np.where(rng.random(n) < f, rng.uniform(0, 1, n), rng.uniform(-1, 0, n))]142    b = np.c_[np.where(rng.random(n) < f, rng.uniform(-1, 0, n), rng.uniform(0, 1, n)), rng.uniform(0, 1, n)]143    return a, b144 145A400, B400 = make_sets(0.2)146X = np.vstack([A400, B400])147y_from_set = np.r_[np.zeros(400), np.ones(400)]          # the label the data carries148y_true = (X[:, 1] > 0).astype(float)                       # the label the concept defines149 150def train_classifier(X, y, steps=1500):151    torch.manual_seed(0)152    net = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(2, 64), torch.nn.SiLU(), torch.nn.Linear(64, 64), torch.nn.SiLU(), torch.nn.Linear(64, 1))153    opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), 3e-3, weight_decay=1e-3)154    Xt, yt = torch.tensor(X, dtype=torch.float32), torch.tensor(y, dtype=torch.float32)[:, None]155    for _ in range(steps):156        opt.zero_grad(); torch.nn.functional.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(net(Xt), yt).backward(); opt.step()157    return net158 159fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4.2))160q = np.linspace(-0.85, 0.85, 9); Q1, Q2 = np.meshgrid(q, q)161for a, y, name in [(ax[0], y_from_set, "labels from set membership"), (ax[1], y_true, "true labels (x2 > 0)")]:162    net = train_classifier(X, y)163    with torch.no_grad():164        pB = torch.sigmoid(net(torch.tensor(grid, dtype=torch.float32))).numpy().reshape(G, G)165    qx = torch.tensor(np.c_[Q1.ravel(), Q2.ravel()], dtype=torch.float32, requires_grad=True)166    torch.nn.functional.logsigmoid(net(qx)).sum().backward()167    gr = qx.grad.numpy(); The other slot holds anything.217#218# - **Centred training data**: every cat image has its cat in slot 1, and so does every dog image. Both experts constrain the same slot, so the product is a product over the same variables where a partition was meant. Its mass sits at $x_1 \approx 0$, a value that is neither cat nor dog. **That is the chimera.** For Gaussians the arithmetic is exact: $\mathcal{N}(-0.5, s^2)\,\mathcal{N}(+0.5, s^2) \propto \mathcal{N}(0, s^2/2)$.219# - **Position-varied training data**: each object appears in either slot. The product now has modes at $(-0.5, +0.5)$ and $(+0.5, -0.5)$, one object per slot, both intact. **The same product operator produces co-occurrence.**220#221# The numbers: "co-occurrence" is the mass where one slot is within 0.15 of $-0.5$ and the other within 0.15 of $+0.5$. "Chimera" is the mass where neither slot is within 0.15 of either object.222 223# %% cell 12 [code]: def obj(v, n, varied):224def obj(v, n, varied):225    o = v + 0.05 * rng.standard_normal(n); other = rng.uniform(-1, 1, n)226    swap = (rng.random(n) < 0.5) if varied else np.zeros(n, bool)227    return np.where(swap[:, None], np.c_[other, o], np.c_[o, other])228 229near = lambda Z, v: np.abs(Z - v) < 0.15230CO = (near(X1, -.5) & near(X2, .5)) | (near(X1, .5) & near(X2, -.5))231CHIMERA = ~(near(X1, -.5) | near(X1, .5) | near(X2, -.5) | near(X2, .5))232 233fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(10, 6.6))234for row, varied in enumerate([False, True]):235    cat, dog = obj(-0.5, 600, varied), obj(0.5, 600, varied)236    lpc, lpd = ideal_expert(cat, 0.2), ideal_expert(dog, 0.2)237    show(ax[row, 0], density(lpc), f"cat expert ({'position-varied' if varied else 'centred'})", region=None)238    show(ax[row, 1], density(lpd), f"dog expert ({'position-varied' if varied else 'centred'})", region=None)239    prod = density(lpc + lpd)240    show(ax[row, 2], prod, f"product\nco-occurrence {mass(prod, CO):.2f} · chimera {mass(prod, CHIMERA):.2f}")241    for a in ax[row]: a.set_xlabel("slot 1"); a.set_ylabel("slot 2")242plt.tight_layout()243 244# %% cell 13 [markdown]: 4c. The dial is set at 0% and at 20%, and the number is the mean $x_1$ of the product's mass in the top half: $-0.8$ means the interaction was produced, and $-0.5$ means a dry dog in the rain.252 253# %% cell 14 [code]: def interaction_sets(f, n=600):254def interaction_sets(f, n=600):255    top = rng.random(n) < f256    a = np.c_[np.where(top, -0.8, -0.5) + 0.06 * rng.standard_normal(n),257              np.where(top, rng.uniform(0, 1, n), rng.uniform(-1, 0, n))]258    hid = rng.random(n) < f259    b = np.c_[np.where(hid, -0.8 + 0.06 * rng.standard_normal(n), rng.uniform(-1, 1, n)), rng.uniform(0, 1, n)]260    return a, b261 262fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 3.4))263for a_, f in zip(ax[:2], [0.0, 0.2]):264    a, b = interaction_sets(f)265    prod = density(ideal_expert(a, 0.08) + ideal_expert(b, 0.08))266    top = X2 > 0267    mean_x1 = (prod * top * X1).sum() / (prod * top).sum()268    show(a_, prod, f"product, overlap {f:.0%}\nmean x1 in top half = {mean_x1:.2f}", region=None)269a, b = interaction_sets(0.2)270ax[2].scatter(*b.T, s=3, c="tab:blue", label="B: rain (top half)")271ax[2].scatter(*a.T, s=3, c="tab:red", label="A: dog (x1=-0.5, wet x1=-0.8 in top)")272ax[2].set_xlim(-L, L); ax[2].set_ylim(-L, L); ax[2].legend(fontsize=7, loc="lower right"); ax[2].set_title("training data at 20% overlap")273plt.tight_layout()274 275# %% cell 15 [markdown]: What this notebook cannot show276# **Reading it.** At 0% overlap, neither expert has seen A under B's influence. 1# %% cell 1 [markdown]: What an expert learns, and the kinds of composition: worked  …2# # What an expert learns, and the kinds of composition: worked examples in 2D3#4# This notebook is the worked examples for claims 1 and 7 of [the overlap-dial idea map](IDEA_MAP.md). The definitions it illustrates are in [the composition terms](composition-terms.md).5#6# Two questions:7#8# 1. **Does expert A care how its training points are labelled?** (claim 1: the example and the break)9# 2. **Are co-occurrence, intersection, contention and interaction different things, and what produces each?** (claim 7)10#11# **No sampler appears anywhere.** In 2D, a product density can be computed exactly on a grid and normalised, so every picture below is the true target. A sampler would add its own error, which is claim 4's subject.12#13# **What an "ideal expert" is here.** A diffusion model trained to optimum on a finite training set, at noise level $\sigma$, has the score of the training points smoothed by a Gaussian:14#15# $$p^{\text{ideal}}_\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathcal{N}(x;\, x_i,\, \sigma^2 I).$$16#17# So every expert below is that formula applied to its training set, with no network trained. This is the best any trained expert can do at noise $\sigma$, which makes every failure below a property of the data or of the composition, never of training.18 19# %% cell 2 [code]: import numpy as np, torch, matplotlib.pyplot as plt20import numpy as np, torch, matplotlib.pyplot as plt21from scipy.special import logsumexp22plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "axes.titlesize": 10})23rng = np.random.default_rng(0); torch.manual_seed(0)24 25L, G = 1.1, 24126xs = np.linspace(-L, L, G)27X1, X2 = np.meshgrid(xs, xs)28grid = np.stack([X1.ravel(), X2.ravel()], 1)29cell = (xs[1] - xs[0]) ** 230TOP_LEFT = (X1 < 0) & (X2 > 0)           # the A∩B region in the quadrant setup31 32def ideal_expert(data, sigma):33    "Log-density on the grid of the training points smoothed by N(0, sigma^2 I)."34    d2 = ((grid[:, None, :] - np.asarray(data)[None]) ** 2).sum(-1)35    lp = logsumexp(-d2 / (2 * sigma**2), axis=1) - np.log(len(data)) - np.log(2 * np.pi * sigma**2)36    return lp.reshape(G, G)37 38def density(logp):39    "Normalise a log-density on the grid so it integrates to 1."40    p = np.exp(logp - logp.max()); return p / (p.sum() * cell)41 42def mass(p, region):43    return float((p * region).sum() * cell)44 45def show(ax, p, title, pts=None, region=TOP_LEFT):46    ax.imshow(p, origin="lower", extent=[-L, L, -L, L], cmap="magma")47    ax.axhline(0, color="w", lw=.4, alpha=.5); ax.axvline(0, color="w", lw=.4, alpha=.5)48    if pts is not None:49        ax.scatter(*np.asarray(pts).T, s=14, c="cyan", edgecolor="k", lw=.4)50    ax.set_title(title); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])51 52# %% cell 3 [markdown]: 1. Example: same points, different labels, same expert53# ## 1. Example: same points, different labels, same expert54#55# Expert A's training set is three points. In **version 1** all three are labelled "A", and the top-left one is secretly also B. In **version 2** the top-left one is labelled "A, B".56#57# The denoising loss expert A minimises is58#59# $$\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{x_0 \sim \text{A's set},\ t,\ \varepsilon}\ \big\| \varepsilon - \varepsilon_\theta(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\varepsilon,\ t) \big\|^2 .$$60#61# **No label appears in it.** The only thing a label could change is which points are in A's set, and here it changes nothing.62 63# %% cell 4 [code]: A_set = np.array([[-0.5, -0.5], [-0.6, -0.4], [-0.5, 0.5]])64A_set = np.array([[-0.5, -0.5], [-0.6, -0.4], [-0.5, 0.5]])65labels_v1 = ["A", "A", "A (secretly B)"]66labels_v2 = ["A", "A", "A, B"]67 68# a tiny denoiser, one gradient step on each version, same seed: the labels are never an input69def one_step_grads(x0):70    torch.manual_seed(1)71    net = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(3, 32), torch.nn.SiLU(), torch.nn.Linear(32, 2))72    x0 = torch.tensor(x0, dtype=torch.float32).repeat(64, 1)73    t = torch.rand(len(x0), 1); abar = torch.cos(t * torch.pi / 2) ** 274    eps = torch.randn_like(x0)75    xt = abar.sqrt() * x0 + (1 - abar).sqrt() * eps76    loss = ((eps - net(torch.cat([xt, t], 1))) ** 2).mean()77    loss.backward()78    return torch.cat([p.grad.flatten() for p in net.parameters()])79 80g1, g2 = one_step_grads(A_set), one_step_grads(A_set)   # version 1 and version 2 feed the same x081print("largest difference between the two versions' gradients:", (g1 - g2).abs().max().item())82 83pA = density(ideal_expert(A_set, sigma=0.15))84fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 3.4))85for a, labs, name in [(ax[0], labels_v1, "version 1 labels"), (ax[1], labels_v2, "version 2 labels")]:86    a.scatter(*A_set.T, s=40, c="tab:red"); a.set_xlim(-L, L); a.set_ylim(-L, L)87    a.axhline(0, c="grey", lw=.5); a.axvline(0, c="grey", lw=.5)88    for (x, y), s in zip(A_set, labs): a.annotate(s, (x, y), (5, 5), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=8)89    a.set_title(name); a.set_aspect("equal")90show(ax[2], pA, f"expert A, both versions\nmass in top-left (A∩B) = {mass(pA, TOP_LEFT):.2f}", A_set)91plt.tight_layout()92 93# %% cell 5 [markdown]: 2. Break, part 1: labels matter to a conditional model (cons …94# **Reading it.** The gradient difference is exactly `0.0`, and the one heatmap serves both versions. A third of expert A's mass sits in the top-left quadrant, because one of its three points is there. **For separately trained experts (construction 2), "hidden B" and "labelled A and B" are the same experiment.**95#96# ## 2. Break, part 1: labels matter to a conditional model (construction 1)97#98# Construction (1) trains one model on everything, conditioned on a label, and composes99#100# $$\nabla \log p(x\mid A) + \nabla \log p(x\mid B) - \nabla \log p(x) \;=\; \nabla \log \frac{p(x\mid A)\,p(x\mid B)}{p(x)} .$$101#102# Now the label decides which points train the condition "A". There are two readings:103#104# - **"contains A"**: every point whose label set includes A trains $p(x\mid A)$.105# - **"exactly A"**: a point labelled {A, B} trains a separate condition {A, B}, and drops out of $p(x\mid A)$.106#107# The pool below is A's three points plus B's three points, one of which is secretly A. Version 2 labels are used throughout.108 109# %% cell 6 [code]: B_set = np.array([[0.5, 0.5], [0.6, 0.4], [-0.4, 0.6]])110B_set = np.array([[0.5, 0.5], [0.6, 0.4], [-0.4, 0.6]])111pool = np.vstack([A_set, B_set])112label_sets = [{"A"}, {"A"}, {"A", "B"}, {"B"}, {"B"}, {"A", "B"}]113 114def condition(c, scheme):115    keep = [c in s if scheme == "contains" else s == {c} for s in label_sets]116    return pool[np.array(keep)]117 118sig = 0.15119lp_all = ideal_expert(pool, sig)120fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(10, 6.6))121for row, scheme in enumerate(["contains", "exactly"]):122    dA, dB = condition("A", scheme), condition("B", scheme)123    pA_c = density(ideal_expert(dA, sig)); pB_c = density(ideal_expert(dB, sig))124    comp = density(ideal_expert(dA, sig) + ideal_expert(dB, sig) - lp_all)125    show(ax[row, 0], pA_c, f'p(x|A), "{scheme}" A: {len(dA)} points\ntop-left mass {mass(pA_c, TOP_LEFT):.2f}', dA)126    show(ax[row, 1], pB_c, f'p(x|B), "{scheme}" B: {len(dB)} points\ntop-left mass {mass(pB_c, TOP_LEFT):.2f}', dB)127    show(ax[row, 2], comp, f'composed p(x|A)p(x|B)/p(x)\ntop-left mass {mass(comp, TOP_LEFT):.2f}')128plt.tight_layout()129 130# %% cell 7 [markdown]: 3. Break, part 2: a classifier learns the hidden-B points as …131# **Reading it.** Under "contains A", the composition puts most of its mass in the top-left quadrant. Under "exactly A", the {A, B} points never train either condition, so both conditionals lose their top-left mass and the composition misses A∩B. Its leftover mass sits near the origin, between A's points and B's points, at a place no training point held. **The meaning of the condition is an axis of the experiment.** It has to be fixed and written down before the overlap dial means anything in construction (1).132#133# ## 3. Break, part 2: a classifier learns the hidden-B points as "not B"134#135# Now a classifier $p(B\mid x)$ is trained, as in classifier guidance. Its labels come from **which set a point was in**, which is the label the data actually carries. A hidden-B point in A's set is therefore labelled "not B".136#137# Each set has 400 points. 20% of A's set lies in the top half (hidden B), and 20% of B's set lies in the left half (hidden A). The arrows show the direction of that push (unit length, so only direction is drawn), and the title gives its average over the top-left quadrant: $(+1, 0)$ is straight right, $(0, +1)$ straight up.138 139# %% cell 8 [code]: def make_sets(f, n=400):140def make_sets(f, n=400):141    a = np.c_[rng.uniform(-1, 0, n), np.where(rng.random(n) < f, rng.uniform(0, 1, n), rng.uniform(-1, 0, n))]142    b = np.c_[np.where(rng.random(n) < f, rng.uniform(-1, 0, n), rng.uniform(0, 1, n)), rng.uniform(0, 1, n)]143    return a, b144 145A400, B400 = make_sets(0.2)146X = np.vstack([A400, B400])147y_from_set = np.r_[np.zeros(400), np.ones(400)]          # the label the data carries148y_true = (X[:, 1] > 0).astype(float)                       # the label the concept defines149 150def train_classifier(X, y, steps=1500):151    torch.manual_seed(0)152    net = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(2, 64), torch.nn.SiLU(), torch.nn.Linear(64, 64), torch.nn.SiLU(), torch.nn.Linear(64, 1))153    opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), 3e-3, weight_decay=1e-3)154    Xt, yt = torch.tensor(X, dtype=torch.float32), torch.tensor(y, dtype=torch.float32)[:, None]155    for _ in range(steps):156        opt.zero_grad(); torch.nn.functional.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(net(Xt), yt).backward(); opt.step()157    return net158 159fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4.2))160q = np.linspace(-0.85, 0.85, 9); Q1, Q2 = np.meshgrid(q, q)161for a, y, name in [(ax[0], y_from_set, "labels from set membership"), (ax[1], y_true, "true labels (x2 > 0)")]:162    net = train_classifier(X, y)163    with torch.no_grad():164        pB = torch.sigmoid(net(torch.tensor(grid, dtype=torch.float32))).numpy().reshape(G, G)165    qx = torch.tensor(np.c_[Q1.ravel(), Q2.ravel()], dtype=torch.float32, requires_grad=True)166    torch.nn.functional.logsigmoid(net(qx)).sum().backward()167    gr = qx.grad.numpy(); gr = gr / (np.linalg.norm(gr, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-12)168    in_tl = (qx.detach().numpy()[:, 0] < 0) & (qx.detach().numpy()[:, 1] > 0)169    push = gr[in_tl].mean(0)170    a.imshow(pB, origin="lower", extent=[-L, L, -L, L], cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=1)171    a.quiver(Q1, Q2, gr[:, 0], gr[:, 1], color="w", scale=14, width=.006)172    a.axhline(0, c="w", lw=.4); Co-occurrence and intersection177# **Reading it.** With the labels the data carries, the classifier is unsure in the top-left quadrant, at about 0.5, because that quadrant holds equal numbers of hidden-B points labelled 0 and hidden-A points labelled 1. Its average push there is `(-0.38, -0.04)`: sideways, with almost no upward component. With the true labels it is `(-0.14, +0.99)`, straight up into B. So inside A∩B, guidance toward B has stopped meaning "more B". Its direction now follows where the label proportions happen to change (leftward toward the edge, rightward near $x_1 = 0$ into B-only), not the concept. **The classifier has learned part of "B" from where the points came from rather than from $x_2$, which is the toy's version of a shortcut**, like a pneumothorax classifier that reads the drain. The dial is set at 0% and at 20%, and the number is the mean $x_1$ of the product's mass in the top half: $-0.8$ means the interaction was produced, and $-0.5$ means a dry dog in the rain.252 253# %% cell 14 [code]: def interaction_sets(f, n=600):254def interaction_sets(f, n=600):255    top = rng.random(n) < f256    a = np.c_[np.where(top, -0.8, -0.5) + 0.06 * rng.standard_normal(n),257              np.where(top, rng.uniform(0, 1, n), rng.uniform(-1, 0, n))]258    hid = rng.random(n) < f259    b = np.c_[np.where(hid, -0.8 + 0.06 * rng.standard_normal(n), rng.uniform(-1, 1, n)), rng.uniform(0, 1, n)]260    return a, b261 262fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 3.4))263for a_, f in zip(ax[:2], [0.0, 0.2]):264    a, b = interaction_sets(f)265    prod = density(ideal_expert(a, 0.08) + ideal_expert(b, 0.08))266    top = X2 > 0267    mean_x1 = (prod * top * X1).sum() / (prod * top).sum()268    show(a_, prod, f"product, overlap {f:.0%}\nmean x1 in top half = {mean_x1:.2f}", region=None)269a, b = interaction_sets(0.2)270ax[2].scatter(*b.T, s=3, c="tab:blue", label="B: rain (top half)")271ax[2].scatter(*a.T, s=3, c="tab:red", label="A: dog (x1=-0.5, wet x1=-0.8 in top)")272ax[2].set_xlim(-L, L); ax[2].set_ylim(-L, L); ax[2].legend(fontsize=7, loc="lower right"); ax[2].set_title("training data at 20% overlap")273plt.tight_layout()274 275# %% cell 15 [markdown]: What this notebook cannot show276# **Reading it.** At 0% overlap, neither expert has seen A under B's influence. The product puts its top-half mass near $x_1 = -0.5$, hugging the boundary $x_2 \approx 0$ where the dog expert's smoothed tail meets the rain: a dry dog at the edge of the rain. At 20% overlap, both experts hold some shifted points, and the product lands near $-0.8$. **The product found the interaction without any extra term, once the data contained it.** This is the evidence behind `break 7`: interaction may be intersection plus a data condition, rather than a third operator.277#278# ## What this notebook cannot show279#280# - **Nothing here was sampled.** Every product is exact on the grid. A real sampler (reverse diffusion or annealed MCMC) adds its own error, and that is claim 4.281# - **The experts are ideal.** A trained network extrapolates differently from Gaussian smoothing, and on images that extrapolation is the whole hope of claim 2. These figures show what the data permits, and say nothing about what a network invents.282# - **Two dimensions only.** "Slots" and "regions" are single coordinates here. Pixels in an image are not independent coordinates, and an object's region is not fixed.
